title: How We Got the Old Testament
subtitle: When the Hebrew canon closed, who says so, and how you would know.
triageNote: That the Old Testament Jesus read is the word of God is common ground for every Christian tradition. When and how its list of books became fixed, and what that process tells us about where canonical authority comes from, is a debate that runs through the scholarship and along the old fault line between the communions. It changes how you answer the skeptic and how you regard the books between the testaments. But it does not divide believer from unbeliever. Hold the books firmly. Hold your theory of the list with the humility the evidence demands. The evidence is real. It does not all point one way.
question: Your Old Testament has thirty-nine books. The Hebrew Bible has the same books counted as twenty-four, arranged in three divisions, the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings. Nobody disputes that by the second century of the Christian era, Jewish communities held a defined collection they regarded as sacred Scripture. The question is when that definition happened. And what kind of event it was. Was the canon substantially closed early, by the time of Ezra or at latest the second century before Christ. So that Jesus inherited a settled Bible. Or did the third division, the Writings, stay soft at the edges into the first and second centuries after Christ, with books like Esther, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs still under discussion in the rabbinic schools. And either way, who had the authority to say, and does the church receive the list from the synagogue or know it through her own life with God.
whyItMatters:
Sooner or later someone will tell you that the Bible's table of contents was decided late, by committees, for political reasons. That other books were suppressed. You will want to know whether that is true. It is mostly not. But the honest answer is more interesting than a slogan. Josephus counted the books in the nineties of the first century, the grandson of Sirach named the three divisions two centuries before Christ, and the rabbis at Yavneh discussed whether Ecclesiastes defiles the hands. A Christian who knows that evidence will be neither bluffed by the skeptic nor tempted to bluff back.

It also matters for what sits between the testaments. Whether the books Protestants call the Apocrypha belong in the canon, the question the next page in this set takes up, turns substantially on the question of this page. If the Hebrew canon was closed before those books could enter it, the Protestant case is strong, and if the canon was still open in the apostles' day, the Catholic and Orthodox case breathes easier. The two debates are one debate viewed from two sides.

And underneath both sits the question that will not stay academic: how would anyone know a book is from God. By a prophet's signature. By a council's vote. By long use in the worshiping community. By the witness of the Spirit. Every answer has consequences. You hold one already, whether or not you have ever said it out loud.

positions.name: Early closure
positions.inOneLine: The Hebrew canon was substantially complete well before Christ, recognized as prophecy was given and ceasing when prophecy ceased. So Jesus inherited and endorsed a settled Bible.
positions.bestCase:
Let me put my strongest witness on the stand first. Around the year 95, the Jewish historian Josephus, defending his people against the Greek scholar Apion, wrote that the Jews do not possess myriads of inconsistent books like the Greeks, but only twenty-two, justly accredited, containing the record of all time. He says the succession of the prophets ran from Moses to Artaxerxes. Books written after that time are not held worthy of equal credit, because the exact succession of the prophets failed, and, most remarkably, in all the long ages no one has dared to add, remove, or alter anything. That is not a man describing a canon under construction. That is a man describing a closed library. And a national instinct about it so old he cannot imagine it otherwise.

Now walk backward from Josephus. Around 132 before Christ, the grandson of Jesus ben Sirach, translating his grandfather's book into Greek, refers three times in his prologue to the Law, the Prophets, and the others that followed them, the rest of the books. The threefold shape of the Hebrew Bible is already standing furniture. And notice the unintended testimony. The grandson knows his grandfather's own excellent book is in a different category from the books. Earlier still, 2 Maccabees preserves the memory of Judas collecting the books scattered by the war, as Nehemiah had founded a library before him. Acts of preservation, not of selection. By the time you reach the New Testament, the evidence speaks with one voice. Jesus says the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, the third division named by its first book. He spans the martyrs from Abel to Zechariah, Genesis to Chronicles, the first and last books of the Hebrew arrangement. The way we say Genesis to Revelation. He and his opponents argue fiercely about everything, purity, sabbath, resurrection, authority, and never once about whether a book belongs in Scripture. Shared canon is the silent premise of every argument in the Gospels.

What about the rabbis at Yavneh around the year 90, discussing Ecclesiastes and the Song. Roger Beckwith's answer, and mine, is that scholastic discussion of books long received is not canonization. The rabbis also debated Ezekiel's compatibility with Moses, and no one thinks Ezekiel entered the canon in the second century. Jack Lewis showed in 1964 that the so-called Council of Jamnia, the supposed synod that fixed the canon, is a scholarly legend. There was no council. No binding ruling. Only school debates about books already inside. The canon did not need a council, because it grew the only way a canon of prophecy can. God spoke. The people of God recognized His voice as He spoke. And when the voice fell silent after Malachi, the collection was, by that very silence, complete. First Maccabees says it plainly. There was great distress in Israel such as had not been since the prophets ceased to appear among them. Israel knew the difference between the books and all other books. That knowledge is the canon.
advocates: Roger Beckwith (The Old Testament Canon of the New Testament Church, 1985)

positions.name: Gradual closure
positions.inOneLine: The Law and the Prophets were fixed early, but the third division remained open-edged into the first and second centuries after Christ, and the tidy early canon is a conclusion read back into mixed evidence.
positions.bestCase:
I want to begin by agreeing with much of what you just heard, because my position is routinely caricatured as canon chaos. It is nothing of the kind. The Torah was bedrock centuries before Christ. The Prophets were a recognized collection by the second century before Christ at the latest. Nobody in my camp doubts that Jesus and Paul had Scriptures, quoted them as God's word, and shared with their hearers a large, stable core. My claim is narrower and, I think, simply what the evidence shows. The edges of the third division, the Writings, were still soft in the first century, and the line was drawn over time, by use and debate. Not all at once, and not before the questions had actually been asked.

Consider what the tidy view has to explain away. At Qumran, the library of a Jewish sect contemporary with Jesus, the book of Enoch and the book of Jubilees turn up in numbers that rival the biblical books. Jubilees is apparently cited as authoritative. And Esther is, on the surviving evidence, absent altogether. The New Testament itself never quotes Esther, Ecclesiastes, or the Song, and Jude quotes Enoch with the formula of prophecy. The Greek-speaking Jews of Alexandria read and transmitted a wider collection, the one that became the church's Septuagint. And the rabbis, into the second century, are recorded debating whether Ecclesiastes, the Song, and even Esther defile the hands. That is their technical term for sacred status. You may call those debates academic exercises about settled books. I ask you to notice that this is precisely what one says when the debates are inconvenient. The simpler reading is that they were debates, about books whose status was genuinely under discussion. The discussion ended, in rabbinic Judaism, in the generations after the temple fell, when a community stripped of land and shrine drew its boundary around the book.

Albert Sundberg changed the field in 1964. His contribution was to break the false equation between the Scriptures the apostles used and a closed canon. First-century Judaism had Scripture, abundantly, reverently. But Scripture as a defined and bounded list is a later achievement. The church inherited the wider, unbounded usage. That is exactly why the church's Old Testament, for its first fifteen centuries, was bigger than the rabbis' Bible. That fact wants explaining. My account explains it without embarrassment. Lee McDonald has assembled the evidence at book length: the canon question received different answers in different Jewish and Christian communities for centuries. None of this disturbs faith unless your faith required the tidy story. The word of God was never in doubt. The exact circumference of the Writings was, for a while. And saying so is not skepticism. It is reading the sources in daylight.

positions.name: Reception through the church
positions.inOneLine: The Old Testament canon is finally known not by reconstructing Jewish decisions but by what the apostolic church received and used, which is why the church's Bible included the wider Greek collection from the beginning.
positions.bestCase:
Both of my friends have been arguing about a Jewish question, when did the synagogue close its list, and I want to put a prior question to you as a Christian. Whose book is the Old Testament. The church did not receive a list from the synagogue, sealed and notarized. The church received Christ, and from Christ a way of reading Israel's Scriptures, beginning with Moses and all the prophets he interpreted to them the things concerning himself. And the church received those Scriptures in the form she actually used, which was overwhelmingly the Greek Bible, the Septuagint, the translation made in Alexandria beginning in the third century before Christ. When the apostles wrote the New Testament, the majority of their Old Testament quotations follow the Greek. When the church spread from Jerusalem to Rome, the Bible she carried, copied, and read at the table was the Greek Bible. Our oldest complete Scriptures survive in the great codices, Vaticanus and Sinaiticus in the fourth century, and they bind Wisdom, Sirach, Tobit, and Judith between the same covers as Isaiah. Without a divider page.

Now, what follows. Not that a translation is inspired and the Hebrew is not. What follows is a doctrine of canon. A canon is not a fact you dig out of Josephus. It is a rule the church lives by. The church knows her Scriptures the way a child knows the voices of her own household, by being raised among them. The Law was read, the Prophets were read, the Wisdom of Solomon was read at the martyrs' feasts, and the worshiping community, century after century, sorted the books that fed her from the books that did not. When the bishops at Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397 listed the canon, they included the books the Reformers would later set apart. They were not inventing. They were writing down the household's long knowledge. Augustine against Jerome, in their famous disagreement, stood exactly here: the usage of the churches, he said, is the weightier authority.

I will be honest about what my position requires. It requires you to believe that the Spirit who breathed the books also guided their gathering. That canonization is providence and not merely paperwork. But notice, every position at this table requires that somewhere. The early-closure men trust the Spirit's work in Israel's recognition. The gradual-closure men describe a human process. They must either trust God in it or surrender the canon to sociology. I simply locate the trust where the New Testament locates the church, as the pillar and buttress of the truth, the household in which the oracles of God are at home. Ask me how I know the list. I will answer the way the whole ancient church would have answered. These are the books that were read when I was baptized, read over the martyrs, read at the eucharist for two thousand years. The voice of the Shepherd is known in His flock.
advocates: the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox traditions
canonical-reception scholars in the wake of Brevard Childs

biblicalEvidence.summary: The risen Jesus says everything written about him in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled. The threefold shape of the Hebrew Bible, with the third division named by its leading book. On the lips of Jesus.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for gradual closure, since Jesus names the three divisions as a known, complete frame of reference.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Gradual closure answers that naming the divisions proves the divisions existed, not that their contents were sealed. It also notes that the Psalms may here mean the Psalter itself rather than the whole Writings. The reception view observes that Jesus defines the collection by its witness to himself, which is the church's principle of canon in miniature.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Jesus charges this generation with all the blood shed from Abel to Zechariah. Abel dies in Genesis. Zechariah son of Jehoiada dies in 2 Chronicles 24, and Chronicles stands last in the traditional Hebrew ordering. The phrase reads like Genesis to the end of the shelf.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for gradual closure, because the saying seems to presuppose a fixed arrangement with Chronicles as the final book.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Gradual closure replies that the argument carries real weight only if the Hebrew ordering with Chronicles last was already standard in the first century. The manuscript and rabbinic evidence cannot confirm that early, and Jesus may simply be spanning the first and last martyrs whose blood cries out in Scripture. Early closure counters that the alternative explanations multiply while the simple one sits in plain sight. The reception view notes the church received the same span with a different book order and lost nothing.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Early closure, with reception claiming the principle
biblicalEvidence.summary: What advantage has the Jew? Much in every way. To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God. Paul locates the custody of the Scriptures with Israel.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any account that detaches the canon entirely from Israel's own recognition, including a version of the reception view that lets the church define the Old Testament without reference to the synagogue.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Early closure draws the Protestant conclusion: the Hebrew canon, as Israel kept it, is the church's Old Testament. That is why Jerome argued for the Hebrew truth. The reception view answers that the entrusting was stewardship of living oracles, not a final list, and that Israel's own Greek-speaking diaspora kept the wider collection. Gradual closure reads the verse as saying nothing about boundaries at all.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Jude quotes the book of Enoch, by name and as prophecy: Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying. A New Testament author cites, with a prophetic formula, a book that no major canon ever received.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for early closure, because an apostle treats a book outside the supposed closed canon as carrying prophetic weight, and hard for the simple rule that citation equals canonicity.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Early closure answers that quotation is not canonization. Paul quotes pagan poets. And Jude can affirm one true saying preserved in Enoch without endorsing the book, exactly as a preacher quotes a hymn. Gradual closure replies that the formula prophesied is stronger than literary garnish and shows the soft edge it claims. The reception view notes that the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, alone, did receive Enoch, which demonstrates its point: reception by the community, not citation, is what finally draws the line.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Shared, with a hidden edge for gradual closure and reception
biblicalEvidence.summary: Timothy has known the sacred writings from childhood. All Scripture is breathed out by God. The classic inspiration text, but it names no list, and Timothy, raised by a Greek-speaking Jewish mother in Lystra, almost certainly knew those writings in Greek.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for anyone who wants the verse to define the canon's contents, which it does not attempt.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Early closure reads the sacred writings as the known Hebrew canon in its Greek dress. Gradual closure and the reception view both observe that the Scriptures of a diaspora childhood were the Septuagint's wider shelf, so the verse quietly blesses the collection the church actually inherited. All sides agree the verse asserts the divine origin of Scripture rather than its census.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Jesus says Scripture cannot be broken, resting an argument on a clause of Psalm 82. The remark presupposes a recognized, authoritative body of writing whose smallest statements bind.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any reconstruction in which Scripture was a loose and negotiable category in Jesus' day.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Gradual closure agrees entirely that Scripture was a firm and authoritative category. It repeats that a firm core is not a closed circumference. The reception view hears in cannot be broken the church's own confidence, and adds that the One who said it, not a list, is the final ground of that confidence.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Early closure, claimed by reception as a pattern
biblicalEvidence.summary: Ezra reads the Book of the Law to the assembly from early morning until midday. The Levites give the sense. The people weep and then celebrate. The earliest full portrait of a community gathered under a recognized written Scripture.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for theories that make canonical consciousness a late invention, since the scene shows it functioning in the fifth century before Christ.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Early closure sees the canon principle operating from Ezra forward, recognition tracking revelation. Gradual closure agrees for the Torah, which was always the fixed center, and notes the scene says nothing about the Writings. The reception view points at the picture itself: a worshiping assembly, a read book, interpreters giving the sense. That is how canon lives. And how it was always known.

weighing:
My judgment, offered tentatively, with the sources open on the desk.

On the historical question, I find the early-closure case stronger at the center and the gradual-closure case honest at the edges. I do not think those two sentences contradict. Josephus is very hard to dismiss. A first-century Jew states a fixed number, a closed succession, and a national habit of leaving the books untouched. And he states it as old news. The New Testament's total silence about canon disputes, in a record full of every other kind of dispute, weighs with me the same way. Jesus argued with men about everything except which books were Scripture. Shared premises are the ones nobody mentions. But Qumran really did treasure Jubilees. Jude really does quote Enoch as prophecy. The rabbis really did debate Ecclesiastes. And the tidy view earns mistrust when it files all of that under exceptions. The shelf had a settled middle and, for a while, a discussed margin. Saying so plainly costs the faith nothing.

On the deeper question, where canonical authority comes from, I find I cannot do without the early-closure principle or the reception insight. The principle, that the people of God recognize the voice of God rather than conferring authority on it, seems to me not just true but necessary, the only account on which the canon is discovered rather than manufactured. The sheep hear the Shepherd's voice. But the reception men are right that the recognizing happened somewhere, in assemblies and lectionaries and long arguments, and that a Protestant who sneers at tradition is sawing off the branch his own table of contents sits on. Somebody handed you the list. Gratitude is more honest than amnesia.

If you press me to the practical point: I read the thirty-nine books as the Old Testament canon, on the ground that seems to me weightiest. The oracles were entrusted to Israel. And the Israel of Jesus' day, by the best evidence we have, kept the shelf Josephus counted. And I hold that conclusion with respect for the believers who count the shelf differently, because the next page in this set belongs to them.
charitableDisagreement:
Each position guards a treasure. Early closure guards the divine origin of canonical authority, that God's word was God's word the day it was given. No committee made it so. Gradual closure guards intellectual honesty, the refusal to defend the faith with a story neater than the evidence. That always costs more later. The reception view guards the communal nature of the faith itself, the truth that nobody reads an unmediated Bible, and that the Spirit's work includes the long, slow sorting done by the worshiping church. A believer can stand in any of these rooms and love the same Scriptures.

Is it a hill to die on. That the Old Testament is the word of God, the Scriptures Jesus called unbreakable, yes, hold that to the end. The historical reconstruction of exactly when the third division's edges hardened is not a hill, it is a field for patient work. The workers in it disagree in peace. Where the question becomes churchly, whether the wider Greek collection belongs inside, the disagreement is real and old and runs between communions, and even there it has not kept Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant from confessing one Lord. Learn the evidence. State it fairly, including the parts that inconvenience your side. The canon has survived twenty centuries of both its enemies and its defenders, and it will survive your honesty about the rough edges. Which is, after all, a kind of trust.

relatedDebates.note: The immediate sequel. If the Hebrew canon closed early, the books between the testaments arrived too late. The Protestant position follows. If the church's reception defines the canon, the wider shelf the early church actually used has standing. The next page in this set gives each communion its strongest voice.

relatedDebates.topic: How we got the New Testament
relatedDebates.note: The same questions, criteria, recognition versus conferral, the role of usage, run through the New Testament's story. With better-preserved evidence and a faster timetable. Reading the two pages together shows which principles each tradition applies consistently.

relatedDebates.topic: The Septuagint and the apostles' quotations
relatedDebates.note: The New Testament usually quotes the Old in Greek, sometimes where the Greek differs from the Hebrew. What that practice implies about inspired translation, the authority of a version, and the church's freedom in citation is its own rich question, touched again on the translations page of this set.
